rules.rule: Export is a second sink, never the only one
rules.how: The data center keeps its own heat-rejection plant (existing chillers and towers) sized for 100% of its heat, with its own redundancy. HeatOS adds a free extra place for the heat to go. Nothing about its cooling design depends on us.

A fail-open valve sits between the data center's loop and the network. If the network trips, loses flow or runs hot, the valve sends all the water back through the data center's own coolers within about 30 seconds. The data center's temperature setpoint is never changed by us.

rules.rule: Never export more than 80% of the heat
rules.how: Its own coolers always carry a base load and stay warm and tested. In this plan the peak hour exports 80.0% of the heat, so the rule is met.
A plate heat exchanger keeps the data center's coolant apart from the network water, so a pipe leak outside cannot reach the computers.

Customers take heat out, so the water that comes back is cooler than what went out. That is free pre-cooling for the data center and the reason the plan frees cooling electricity (see the data-center benefits).

match_scorecard.headline: Every customer lifts the heat with a heat pump, at an average COP of 5.3
match_scorecard.how: The data center's water is at about 27 C. Low-temperature users (greenhouses, radiant floors, new buildings, mild-weather radiators) take it directly. Hot water (60 C) and cold-weather radiators get a heat pump that lifts only the difference, so the less lift, the less electricity.

match_scorecard.headline: Peak export 8.2 MW against 8.5 MW available (97.3%)
match_scorecard.how: Checked for every hour of 12 typical days: the heat customers can draw never exceeds what the data center can give. Each heat pump covers only part of its building's coldest hour; the boiler covers the rest.

match_scorecard.headline: Winter export is 99% flat across the day (average / peak)
match_scorecard.how: Computers make heat all day. Homes peak morning and evening, offices by day, hotels and hot-water users run through the night. Mixing them flattens the draw so it matches a flat supply; the tiers decide who goes first if it ever does not.

match_scorecard.headline: 95% of the data center's heat is used in winter, 41% in summer; 47% of delivered heat is year-round load
match_scorecard.how: Heating demand follows the weather; hot water and process heat (such as a greenhouse) do not. Customers are chosen with their summer baseload in mind, so the summer heat is used rather than wasted.

match_scorecard.headline: 99.88% expected network availability; every customer keeps its boiler
match_scorecard.how: Expected time off the network comes from failure rates (data center trip, a break on the customer's own pipe path, building equipment). Storage rides through short trips, valves isolate a broken branch, and the customer's boiler starts by itself within about 10 minutes. Protected and firm customers are the last to be cut when supply is short.

architecture_why: Dense urban blocks, few places for a central plant: a low-temperature loop needs only a heat exchanger at the data center and a heat pump in each basement.
Water stays close to ground temperature, so the pipes lose very little heat and can be plain plastic. A conventional 80/50 C hot-water network would lose several times more on the same route.
Every customer lifts the heat to exactly the temperature it needs (hot water 60 C, radiators 42 to 65 C), so no heat is over-boosted.
The same loop can later carry heat back from offices in summer or deliver cooling, so the pipe works all year.
Equipment goes indoors above the flood line and is built to the area's noise limit (the block is already at 56 dB).

capture_options.name: Condenser-water loop of the cooling plant
capture_options.why: Warm enough for a low-lift heat pump, a simple plate heat exchanger in the plant room, and no change to how the computers are cooled.

capture_options.name: Chilled-water return
capture_options.why: Too cold: the heat pumps would have to lift it much further, using more electricity.

capture_options.name: Liquid cooling taken straight from the racks
capture_options.why: Best heat quality, but it needs each tenant's equipment changed; a carrier hotel is mostly air-cooled today.

users.why: Big, steady hot-water load all year plus winter heating; many residents per connection.

regenerative_scorecard.site_says: The two nearest power plants emit 654 lb CO2 per MWh; one sits beside a disadvantaged community.
regenerative_scorecard.plan_does: Heat pumps move 4 to 5 units of heat per unit of electricity, so the plan still cuts carbon on today's dirtier local grid, and cuts more as the grid cleans up.

regenerative_scorecard.headline: 17.0 million gallons of cooling water saved per year, if the towers are evaporative
regenerative_scorecard.site_says: Water stress is low-medium, groundwater table decline is medium, and runoff reaches the Hudson River (79th percentile direct discharge, impaired waterway, IR rating 5).
regenerative_scorecard.plan_does: Heat we carry away is heat the data center does not reject through cooling towers, so less water is evaporated and less tower blowdown goes to the river. Needs the operator to confirm tower use.

regenerative_scorecard.headline: Heating demand -10% by 2050; year-round share of delivered heat 53%

regenerative_scorecard.plan_does: Warmer winters shrink space heating but not hot water, so the plan favors year-round hot-water customers, and the loop can also cool buildings in hotter summers (not valued yet). Heat pumps and controls go above grade, out of the flood zone.

regenerative_scorecard.headline: 1 public-housing or disadvantaged-community building gets 69% of the heat
regenerative_scorecard.site_says: West of the site, poverty is at the 83rd percentile and minority population at the 79th; the area's social vulnerability is at the 79th percentile.
regenerative_scorecard.plan_does: Public housing is a protected tier: its heat is never cut and it gets extra discount. Equity-flagged buildings rank earlier in the build order.

regenerative_scorecard.headline: Site is already at 56 dB (park baseline 43.9 dB)
regenerative_scorecard.site_says: Sustained noise is 12 dB above the ecological baseline.
regenerative_scorecard.plan_does: Design rule: heat pumps go indoors (basements or enclosures) with a noise limit, and each building's boiler runs less. No new outdoor machinery on the street.

buildings.tier_note: Public housing and affordability-priority homes. Heat is never cut. Discounted price (grants + equity).

Close to the data center (234 m), so the pipe is short.
